The Pesquet parrot (Psittrichas fulgidus), endemic to the montane rainforests of New Guinea, exhibits several reproductive parameters that reflect its specialized lifestyle. Under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic period (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), females typically lay a single clutch of two eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = two eggs per nesting attempt], with only one such clutch produced annually [F_R_i = one such clutch produced annually]. This low reproductive output, equivalent to approximately two eggs per year, is consistent with a slow life-history strategy characteristic of many large-bodied frugivorous psittacines. The energetic demands of producing these eggs are substantial, and the prolonged period of parental care that follows places further constraints on the species’ overall reproductive potential. Field records indicate that this modest fecundity is offset by comparatively high nestling survival rates, a trade-off that is common among altricial rainforest birds. The incubation period itself, however, demands careful thermal regulation, and the duration of embryonic development is known to be influenced by the temperature at which the eggs are maintained.

Neonatal mass in this species is modest relative to the eventual adult size. Newly hatched chicks weigh approximately 15 grams [Wwb = approximately 15 grams], a value that underscores the altricial condition of the nestling at hatching. This initial mass is significantly lower than the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults, which is reported to be 865 grams [Wwi = 865 grams]. The dramatic increase in body mass from hatching to adulthood, representing more than a fifty-fold gain, necessitates a prolonged period of intense parental provisioning. The nestling phase is characterized by rapid feather development and skeletal growth, demanding a steady supply of fruits and flowers. Observations of captive birds suggest that the growth trajectory is steady, though the rate can be influenced by food availability and ambient temperature. The comparatively low hatchling mass may be an adaptation to reduce the energetic burden on the incubating female, allowing her to forage more effectively during the brief incubation recesses. This pattern of a relatively small chick at hatching is a common strategy among parrots that produce small clutches.

Eggs of the Pesquet parrot are incubated at a specific temperature for successful development. The incubation period, or the age at hatching, lasts for 30.5 days [ab = 30.5 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This incubation duration is relatively long compared to other psittacines of equivalent body size, which may be related to the relatively low incubation temperature employed by the species. The precise thermal control exercised by the incubating adult is critical for proper embryonic development, and deviations from this optimal temperature can result in developmental delays or reduced hatchling viability. After hatching, the altricial chicks are brooded intensively by the female, who relies on the male for food delivery. This biparental care system is essential for maintaining the thermal environment necessary for the nestlings’ survival and growth. The 36 °C incubation temperature likely represents a physiological optimum that balances developmental rate with the energetic costs of maintaining egg temperature in the cool, montane environment.

Following hatching, the nestling period progresses through several distinct milestones. The first major transition occurs when the chick leaves the nest, with fledging occurring at 90 days after birth [tx = 90 days after birth] at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This developmental landmark is reached under the typical active body temperature of 41.3 °C exhibited by the species. The approximately three-month nestling period is one of the longest recorded among parrots of comparable size, reflecting the slow development of this specialized frugivore. During this time, the nestling undergoes a complete transformation from a helpless, downy chick to a fully feathered juvenile capable of sustained flight. The parents continue to provision the fledgling for several weeks after it leaves the nest, teaching it to identify and process the hard fruits that form the bulk of its diet. The attainment of flight marks a critical step toward independence, though the young bird remains dependent on its parents for food and protection for an extended period thereafter, a pattern typical of long-lived, K-selected species.

The slow life history of this species extends to its reproductive maturation and overall lifespan. Puberty, defined as the onset of sexual maturity, is reached at 270 days after birth [tp = 270 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. However, despite reaching physiological maturity at this relatively young age, the first successful breeding attempt is typically deferred. The time since birth at first brood is recorded as 3 years [tR = 3 years], with males often not successfully breeding until 5 years of age at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between reaching reproductive competence and initiating breeding is a common feature among large parrots and is likely linked to the time required to acquire a territory, establish a pair bond, and develop the foraging skills necessary to support offspring. Once breeding begins, the maximum recorded longevity for this species is 25 years [am = 25 years], a remarkable lifespan for a bird of its size at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This combination of delayed reproduction, extended parental care, and a long adult lifespan represents a classic slow life-history strategy that is particularly sensitive to environmental perturbation and adult mortality.
